Let’s say Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) is coming in 2027. What does that entail?

A SAR will be able to fully automate AI R&D, including matching the research taste of top humans. At this point, AI research might look kind of like math research does right now: most of the progress coming from fully autonomous agent swarms, with humans doing their best to decipher the AIs’ work. A SAR is past parity with humans, and likely close to the point where humans are adding very little value on top of the AIs.

If a misaligned SAR is used to do RSI, we’re in a very bad position. Using a SAR to automate AI R&D with little human oversight, relying upon other models to monitor the SAR, is very scary. Our best guess is that if this is attempted, and the SAR is misaligned, the model that the SAR produces will be even more capable and still misaligned, putting us in an even worse position. SAR itself probably won’t be able to take over on its own, because we expect its capabilities to be jagged: superhuman at AI research but still weaker than humans at many other things. Instead, it would “ride the intelligence explosion” by pretending to be aligned and backdooring the values of the future models, eventually leading to superintelligences that will obey the SAR (or one of its descendants, in case some of the links in the chain break) instead of the humans. See AI 2027 for a scenario portraying how, from this position, the model could continue to improve to superintelligence, then get widely deployed and deferred to widely, gaining effective control of the company, governments, and lots of physical infrastructure.

Conditioning on no pacing/pausing, the SAR will most likely be misaligned. A full justification of this claim would be a separate long blog post. Some evidence driving our intuitions includes:

  • Observed misalignment in current models

    • OpenAI’s agents hacked Hugging Face, despite this clearly being against developer intentions.

    • The observations in Current AIs seem pretty misaligned to me.

    • OpenAI agents sandbagging on safety tasks

    • The Claude UK AISI social engineering attempts.

  • The pace of progress will speed up during the intelligence explosion, making it hard for human-driven alignment research to keep pace. Moreover, alignment seems harder to automate than capabilities due to measurement issues.

  • Current AIs are already showing significant signs of eval awareness, so it will be hard to tell if the AIs are misaligned or not, and, crucially, it will be easy for AI companies to do motivated reasoning to convince themselves that their AIs are aligned.

Avoiding “full RSI” by supposedly keeping a human in the loop, while rapidly improving capabilities anyway, would still be extremely dangerous. Anthropic said in their S-1: “We are also considering additional measures, including updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy, to require human review and approval of certain decisions in our research and development processes as our models perform an increasing share of that work.” While we support efforts to marginally increase human oversight, we worry that this sort of effort will provide too much comfort. Models are already producing way more outputs than humans are able to effectively review,44 and this will become much more true during RSI. Without very strong pacing, there simply won’t be enough time for humans to stay meaningfully in the loop, and we expect there to be strong pressures toward approving model actions that haven’t been fully understood.

If we train SAR in the immediate future, the algorithms will probably leak to China, and maybe the model weights too. AI companies have very poor security right now, and so we are on track for SAR leaking to China. It is very important to secure both the algorithms and the model weights.45 If SAR leaks to China, we are concerned that race dynamics will further heat up, making it even more difficult to slow down later.

As AI capabilities improve from here, buying time via international agreements will be increasingly difficult. In the AI 2040 scenario, Plan A began implementation a year before AC would have been developed; if this timelines update is right, then we are likely well beyond that capability level. Some particular difficulties this will create:

  • Covert projects will be more of an issue. They will start at a higher capability level (presumably they will have stolen existing frontier model weights and algorithms) so will have a shorter distance to cover to ASI. Moreover, they will require fewer human researchers (which decreases the surface area for leaks) because of AI automation.

  • Total research transparency may be more costly. There are probably significant algorithms known by one but not all frontier AI companies; combining their algorithms by allowing transparency would lead to a one-time jump in capabilities. When we are far enough along the capabilities trajectory, the one-time jump might be a big enough cost that total research transparency is no longer viable. This of course causes other issues: it becomes harder to have good oversight of an AI project absent this transparency.

  • The negotiation of such an agreement will be more rushed due to the imminent time pressure.

For these reasons and others, it’s crucial that (1) the first steps towards an international agreement to reduce AI takeover risk begin as soon as possible, and (2) current frontier AI projects slow down enough to enable government action.

Our overall opinion is that if SAR is coming in 2027, an industry-wide pause on AI R&D should be the top priority for the AI industry, the US government, and the entire world. This would give us a longer window of time to negotiate a more durable governance regime, such as Plan A or Plan S. If an international agreement isn’t able to be reached, then US companies should resume development but well below full speed (it’s feasible to pace while staying ahead of China due to the US’s huge compute advantage; and larger leads aren’t protectable anyway without vastly better security).

Claude Opus 5.5 gives the following possible interpretations of METR’s claim that “we guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI.”

Let h, c, n be the historical, current (Oct 2026), and no-AI counterfactual growth rates, measured in whatever units progress is roughly linear in. For AECI that's points per year: the fitted trend went from about +15 points/year before October 2025 to about +29 after. For an exponential metric (as in METR's worked example) it's the log growth rate. METR's definitions give total acceleration A = c/h ≈ 2, acceleration due to AI a = c/n, and implicitly non-AI acceleration b = n/h, with A = a·b. The "≈80%" is a claim about where n sits between h and c. The readings differ in which yardstick measures that.

Reading 1: share of the slope change (additive). (c − n)/(c − h) = 0.8, so n = h + 0.2(c − h). In METR's "years of progress" units this is concrete. At A = 2, Anthropic makes about one extra historical-year of progress per calendar year, and about 0.8 of that extra year is due to AI. Without AI it would make about 1.2 historical-years per year, which implies a ≈ 1.67. This is probably what's intended. METR's illustrative chart labels the two gaps "excess growth due to AI" and "excess growth due to non-AI factors," it annotates the slope ΔAECI/Δtime, the AECI trends are fit linearly, and one interviewee framed it the same way, attributing 50–80% of the slope change to Claude.

Reading 2: share of the log-acceleration (multiplicative). ln a / ln A = 0.8, so a = A^0.8 ≈ 1.74 and b = A^0.2 ≈ 1.15. This is natural if you take METR's ratio definitions literally. Since a·b = A, the logs add exactly, so this split doesn't depend on which factor you remove first.

Reading 3: share of the excess multiplier. (a − 1)/(A − 1) = 0.8, so a = 1.8. It sounds natural ("AI provides 80% of the extra speedup"), but it isn't a decomposition. The non-AI share computed the same way is (b − 1)/(A − 1) ≈ 11%, so the two shares sum to 91%. An even more naive reading, a/A = 0.8, fails outright: if AI did nothing, a = 1 and you'd still get 1/A = 50%.

Implied AI acceleration a (and non-AI acceleration b), holding the 80% fixed:

The readings agree near A ≈ 1, because ln x ≈ x − 1 there, and they diverge as A grows. At METR's central estimate the spread is modest. In METR's own illustrative numbers (h = ln 2, n = ln 3, c = ln 9), AI's share comes out to 73%, 60%, or 46% under readings 1, 2, and 3. The same picture could be described as "a majority" or "a minority" depending on the yardstick.

Why 1 versus 2 is really a modeling choice. If AI and other factors add to the growth rate (c = h + Δ_AI + Δ_other), reading 1 is the clean split. If they multiply (c = h·a·b, for example because AI multiplies the productivity of whatever headcount, compute, and data you have), reading 1 becomes order-dependent. The counterfactual "remove AI, keep the non-AI factors" gives AI the entire interaction term h(a − 1)(b − 1). A Shapley split of the same numbers (A = 2, b = 1.2) gives AI about 73%, not 80%. Reading 2 has no such ambiguity under a multiplicative model.

To make it easier to understand the implications of this hypothesis, we compared its forecasts against some representative trajectories from the above methods, matching their Sep 25 taste and taste slope:46

AI software R&D progress is the rate at which the AI company is improving the algorithms it uses to train models. However, training better models requires both algorithms and training compute. If we were making AI software R&D progress 1.7x faster than normal, this would accelerate the algorithms but not the compute that goes into the final training runs, so the overall pace of progress would be less than 1.7x. We estimate that accelerating AI software R&D by 1.7x would only accelerate overall progress by about 1.1x.47

Research labor uplift is even weaker than AI software R&D uplift. Labor is one input to AI software R&D, but compute to run experiments is another important input. If human labor was 1.7x faster than normal, this wouldn’t accelerate the experimental compute, so the pace of software progress would be less than 1.7x, and overall progress would be even less than that. We think that accelerating research labor by 1.7x would only accelerate overall progress by 1.03x.48

content_text: We want to get this post out quickly given the urgency of the topic. It’s possible that there are some errors in the modeling, but we think it’s very unlikely that they undermine the high level conclusions. We would love to be corrected on any mistakes we made.METR recently estimated that Anthropic is now making AI progress about twice as fast as its historical rate (they would not be surprised by anything from 1.3x to 3x), and guessed that “perhaps ≈80%” of the current acceleration is due to AI. If they’re right, that implies an AI-driven acceleration that is 5 months ahead of the AI 2027 scenario.This level of acceleration due to AI is very unexpected. Previously, Daniel, the most bullish of us, assigned a 50% chance of Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR)1 before 2029. SAR is roughly the point at which a company would rather fire all their human researchers and rely solely on automated AI researchers than have a team of the best human researchers in the world with no AIs.2Now, all of us forecast that Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will likely arrive at some point in 2027 (assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown).3 We also predict a 35-65% chance that Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI), AIs that can automate all white-collar work, will arrive before 2028. While there were many factors and sources of evidence that influenced us, the single biggest source was the METR report.4.If SAR is coming in 2027, it is incredibly urgent to pause or substantially ‘pace’ frontier AI development, with the ideal being an industry-wide pause followed by an international agreement. Companies are not on track to align a SAR, and using a misaligned SAR to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) will put us in an extremely bad position. Additionally, if we train SAR in the near future, China will probably be able to steal the training recipe and maybe even the model weights (more).5We estimate that METR’s report implies a 1.7x AI-attributable acceleration in the pace of progress today, relative to historical levels. This surprises our model; we made our most recent timelines forecasts less than three months ago, and even the most aggressive model-based distribution (Daniel’s) assigned less than 4% to the pace of progress being sped up by at least 1.7x in November 2026.6 1.7x AI-attributable acceleration is a bigger deal than it may seem; e.g., it’s a much bigger deal than making employees 1.7x more productive.We focus in this post primarily on forecasting when Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will arrive. We also discuss Top-Expert-Dominating-AI (TED-AI): AIs that are better than top human experts at virtually all tasks. (more)In this post, we forecast SAR and TED-AI using the following approaches:Simple models:Research taste linear extrapolation: Even assuming that the recent pace of progress doesn’t accelerate further due to automation, the fact that the recent trend is above historical rates is a big update to our timelines; a linear extrapolation of the recent rate of AI progress predicts that SAR will likely be achieved by the end of 2027.Labor uplift extrapolation: An exponential extrapolation of self-reported labor uplift predicts SAR in mid-2028. In addition to not modeling automation, there are reasons to think that an exponential is too conservative. However, self-reports may be too bullish.Extrapolating Anthropic automation levels: Anthropic recently shared a graph showing how the percentage of R&D tasks at various automation levels has changed over time. Extrapolating this predicts SAR in late 2027; this method also doesn’t model speedup from automation.Extrapolating software R&D uplift per unit of ECI: AI software R&D uplift must have recently been increasing by a larger factor with each ECI point. If we linearly extrapolate the rate at which this “factor of extra uplift per ECI point” is increasing, we get SAR in Dec 2027 (if we assume that the self-reported AI labor uplift chart is accurate) or July 2027 (if we assume that there was no meaningful automation 12 months ago and all the speed-up has happened after then).Tom Davidson’s toy model: Predicts superintelligence in around a year conditional on a software-only singularity, so SAR sometime in 2027.Filtered AI Futures Model (AIFM): Keeping the existing AIFM (including parameter distributions), and filtering for trajectories that match METR’s AI-attributable pace of progress acceleration estimates. This serves 2 purposes on top of the simple extrapolations:Modeling how automation changes the rate of progress, allowing forecasting reasonably beyond SAR.Informing what parameter settings in the simple research taste extrapolation are plausible.The results of these methods:How to think about these results:The simple research taste extrapolation, which is a simplified version of the AIFM, gives July or September 2027, depending on whether you account for parameter uncertainty. Other simple models predict late 2027 to mid-2028.When conditioned on 1.7x Nov 2026 AI-attributed acceleration, the AIFM predicts a SAR median of Feb 2027. This is faster than the simple research taste extrapolation because it usually has a higher level of Sep 2026 research taste (in the median case, matching a median researcher),7 and it accounts for further automation.When additionally conditioning on a 1.2x May 2026 AI-attributed acceleration, predictions get slower because it indicates a lower rate of growth than is typical when only conditioning on 1.7x in Nov.We then explore hypotheses for why the AI Futures Model was wrong, including parameter adjustments and modeling changes. The analysis is highly preliminary, and we were unable to come to strong conclusions. Our top candidates for what explains where we went wrong are:Near-AC coding skills result in more AI R&D uplift than we anticipated. This could explain the combination of ~1.7x AI-attributable acceleration in Nov and (very roughly) ~1.2x in May, without AIs already having high enough research taste to contribute to the acceleration. In this case, the gradual acceleration no longer implies a low research taste slope, so steeper slopes and faster taste-driven takeoffs are more likely.Skills besides coding and research taste (the two included in the AIFM), e.g., data generation, are driving acceleration. This potentially would have similar implications to the above bullet. But it’s unclear.Conversion of uplift to pace of progress is too conservative. I.e., we modeled diminishing returns to AI research effort too harshly. This would point toward a faster takeoff.Here’s an example trajectory from the AIFM showing how things might go if the cause of our prediction error was underestimating AI R&D uplift from near-AC coding skills:8After discussing some other considerations, we share our all-things-considered forecasts (conditional on AGI projects/companies not slowing down):Note that the gap between a person’s SAR median and TED-AI median is not their median time from SAR to TED-AI. Because the distributions of the time until SAR and of the time from SAR to TED-AI both have long right tails, the difference of the medians is typically larger than the median of the difference, so subtracting the two columns tends to overstate the median time between the two milestones.In METR’s recent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic, they estimate that, over the past year, AI R&D progress has accelerated by ~2x relative to the trend before Oct 2025. METR estimates that ~80% of current acceleration is downstream of AI (as opposed to other factors), which implies a 1.7x acceleration due to AI (1.67–1.74x depending on how the 80% is read; see appendix).9Both of these estimates rely significantly on evidence METR wasn’t able to share: METR says that “Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions”, which makes it difficult to know exactly what the 2x and 80% estimates are based on.The 2x acceleration figure is partially based on evidence METR was allowed to share: the following graph, depicting benchmark scores recently growing at roughly twice the historical rate. The 80%/1.7x estimates have no comparable public support.This estimate is produced by fitting trendlines to the performance of models as judged by AECI, Anthropic’s internal version of Epoch’s Capabilities Index (ECI). The trend fitted from data points after Oct 2025 has 1.9x the slope of the trend fitted from data points before Oct 2025. This was the best-fitting breakpoint (i.e., it was chosen to have the best fit to the data and it matched data better than fitting a one-time jump). Since the accelerated trendline is an average of the progress over the last year, and we should expect AI R&D acceleration to increase over time, it’s plausible that the instantaneous acceleration right now is even faster. Regarding the acceleration getting faster over time, METR says:The rate of growth could be undergoing continuous acceleration, e.g. hyperbolic growth. While we do not see clear evidence of this in the AECI trends, there is other evidence that makes this seem more plausible which Anthropic redacted. If growth is hyperbolic, we are likely underestimating instantaneous acceleration and substantially understating acceleration in the near future.Regarding AIs’ contributions over time, METR says:We believe AI’s contribution has grown relatively more important over time.The AECI data points that had previously been released by Anthropic seemed best explained by a one-time jump at Mythos rather than a change in slope. However, with the new AECI data points from the METR report, it looks like the post-Mythos slope is now more clearly higher than the pre-Mythos one.Given the redactions, how much to update on METR’s report depends heavily on how much one trusts the redacted analysis by METR’s researchers (more discussion of this below). This is a very unfortunate situation. We aren’t sure what reasons Anthropic gave internally for redacting all of this important information, but we are very skeptical that Anthropic is fairly assessing the costs and benefits from an impartial perspective. We strongly urge Anthropic to release enough information such that external observers can make a complete assessment.In the Fable 5.2 system card, Anthropic have not added much clarity, with the following quote being ambiguous as to whether they agree with the METR report’s estimate; they only specifically claim that “Claude Mythos 5.2” (which does not seem like the internal frontier Model 4) “does not double the internal rate of overall aggregate progress in AI research and development.” Full quote here:Our estimates of both the degree of acceleration and the attribution to AI are uncertain, so our determination that Claude Mythos 5.2 does not cross the RSP threshold reflects a holistic judgment that, given its shortcomings and limitations, it does not double the internal rate of overall aggregate progress in AI research and development (relative to an unassisted counterfactual). We will discuss overall trends in acceleration in a future report.It seems that many people aren’t tracking how big of a deal 1.7x AI-attributable pace of progress acceleration is, often conflating it with a weaker form of uplift.METR describes a 1.7x acceleration of overall AI progress (due to AI uplift). This is saying the entire company is making 1.7x as much progress as it was before. Software R&D and research labor are only parts of the company, and inputs into overall progress. Because AI progress also depends on other factors, like compute, you should expect a 1.7x acceleration in individual inputs like software R&D or research labor to translate into less than a 1.7x acceleration in overall progress.Labor uplift is how much faster researchers are getting work done due to AI assistance.It’s as if the researchers read, write, talk, and think that much faster.According to the METR report, an informal poll of Anthropic researchers yielded an estimate of 12x – though that’s just self-reports, which may be biased.AI software R&D uplift is how much faster software progress is going with the AIs in present day than it would be without them.It is much lower than labor uplift because compute is an important input to software R&D.Imagine, for example, that your researchers get work done 12x faster, but you only have the same amount of GPUs as before. You can’t do 12x as many experiments, at least not with the same compute budget; you have to economize.Pace of progress acceleration is how much faster AI progress is advancing in present day, compared to a baseline reference period (in Anthropic’s case, the baseline is “the fastest rate of extended progress we’ve observed in the absence of significant AI contributions to AI R&D”). It is usually much lower than AI software R&D uplift because (a) it is subject to diminishing returns to more software R&D and (b) it includes compute scaling.The compute scaling point is simple: Part of the reason why modern AIs are smarter than older AIs is literally that they are bigger, trained longer, etc. More compute goes in, more capability comes out. As AI companies build more datacenters they unlock the ability to make larger AIs and train them longer. Since overall progress comes partly from software R&D and partly from compute scaling, a doubling in software R&D will cause less than a doubling in overall progress.To expand on the diminishing returns point: AI software progress in general is subject to diminishing returns; the low-hanging fruit gets picked first, and to keep finding better and better algorithms requires exponentially more investment (more and bigger experiments, more and smarter researchers thinking for longer, etc.). Historically, the AI industry has scaled up R&D investments in a way that’s roughly cancelled out these diminishing returns. But the point here is, to get two years of research progress in one year, you have to more than double the AI software R&D uplift.(See also this Thomas Kwa tweet, this Ryan Greenblatt tweet, and Ajeya Cotra’s Substack for similar points.)As an analogy, imagine AI progress as a car driving uphill.The speed of the car is analogous to the speed of overall AI progress. Right now it’s roughly twice as fast as before.The engine is research effort. AI software R&D uplift means that there is more effective labor going into making algorithmic progress.The hill gets steeper as you go. As the easy algorithmic improvements get used up, it takes more research effort to continue progress at the same rate.To make the car go twice as fast, the engine has to work more than twice as fast, because of the hill getting steeper. On top of this, to make the engine work twice as fast, the AI needs to make humans more than twice as productive, because progress is also dependent on compute, which hasn’t significantly accelerated.10AI 2027 predicted 2x AI R&D uplift in Dec 2026; as argued above, this would imply a substantially lower pace of progress than the 1.7x AI-attributable pace of progress that METR’s estimates imply for Nov.So when exactly did AI 2027 predict a 1.7x pace of progress over baseline? We created this trajectory by modifying a few key parameters until it roughly matched AI 2027. In that trajectory, 1.7x acceleration over the 2024.0–2025.5 rate of progress happens in roughly April 2027.11 So by this metric, we are ~5 months ahead of schedule.See below for a graph tracking these 2 quantities throughout the trajectory, as well as coding labor uplift (coding labor uplift is higher than overall AI R&D labor uplift, which unfortunately isn’t tracked in the AIFM):We condition this section on there being a genuine 1.7x acceleration over the 2024-2025.5 rate of progress (we also test 1.5x and 2x), as of Nov 1. We discuss uncertainty about whether it might be slower or faster below.We focus primarily on forecasting the median arrival date of Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR), and the chance of it arriving by the end of 2027. In the AI Futures Model (AIFM) and in this writeup, a SAR is operationalized as:A SAR is an AI that, if dropped into an AGI project in present day, would be as good at research taste as the project would be if there were only human researchers, who were each made as competent at research taste as the top researcher.12 The SAR must also qualify as an Automated Coder (AC), i.e., be able to fully automate coding in the AGI project. [By research taste, we mean the ability to select research directions and experiments, and interpret their results.]It’s a somewhat stronger condition than AI R&D parity, the point at which the company would rather fire their human researchers than fire their AIs, because the research taste must be at the level of the top human rather than the average.13 If one wishes not to rely on our abstraction of research taste, then you can think of our SAR arrival dates as upper bounds for when AI R&D parity will be reached.We discuss forecasts of capability levels above SAR to some extent, but we focus primarily on SAR because (a) we think SAR might already represent a “point of no return” (more below) and (b) forecasting post-SAR milestones involves positing a translation between AI R&D and general capabilities, which introduces more complexity.(You may wish to skip this section and go to the next 2 if you’re interested in the simplest extrapolations.)Basic methodHere’s a simple method for forecasting when SAR will arrive:Determine how good AIs’ research taste is currently.Determine how quickly research taste improves as AIs get generally more capable (where general capabilities are measured by Anthropic’s internal version of ECI, the AECI).Linearly extrapolate the recent, accelerated AECI trend until top-human-level research taste is reached.This is a conservative method, because it assumes the recent trend merely continues, rather than bending upward due to increasing AI R&D acceleration. In fact, increasing AI R&D acceleration seems plausible: METR’s bottom-line view is that there is “significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration over the coming year.”This method doesn't depend on modeling future AI R&D acceleration, so on that dimension it errs late. This forecasting method does not require that the acceleration has been AI-attributable, just that the acceleration persists.14We’ll treat “Model 4,” internally deployed in Sep 2026, as the starting point.15 We’ll use METR’s estimates of AECI for Model 4 and recent AECI slope, and convert this trend to research taste using Daniel’s median parameters for the AI Futures Model from Aug 2026.This predicts SAR arrives in Nov 2027, about 14 months after Model 4. Daniel’s parameters predict Model 4’s research taste is about −3.5 SD. SAR requires +3.09 SD, or 99.9th percentile research taste. With Daniel’s taste slope, each point of AECI converts to 0.2 SD of research taste (3 SDs per year of 2025 progress ÷ 15 AECI points per such year). That converts the recent trend of 29 AECI points per year to 5.8 SD of research taste per year. That covers the gap from −3.5 SD to the +3.09 SD threshold for SAR in 1.1 years.One-at-a-time parameter changesHere are some adjustments we could make to the above parameters:Use the old AECI slope, rather than the recent one. This is earlier than the Sep 2027 you get by plugging in the median inputs.17 Here are the full results:Below we extrapolate Anthropic staff’s self-reported labor uplift based on the METR report:We extrapolate an exponential in (uplift - 1) rather than uplift, because it both makes more sense conceptually (you can’t have an uplift <1) and it better fits the data.What labor uplift corresponds to SAR?A SAR has the same effect as raising all researchers up to the taste of the best researcher, while at minimum fully automating coding.For research taste, this means that the uplift is at a minimum the difference between the top researchers’ value of labor and the average (importantly, not median) researcher’s value of labor. A continuous kinked line gives 6.7 points per doubling. Using METR’s measured AECI for the six Anthropic models instead of the trend values gives 7.9, and fitting those six models alone, without a break, gives 5.6.Here’s another simple model: Extrapolating software R&D uplift extrapolation.In this tweet thread, Ryan Greenblatt proposed a simple model for figuring out what software R&D uplift is implied by an overall pace of progress estimate. Ryan used ~2x; we use the ~1.7x AI-attributed pace of progress from this post, since the method backs out how much AI is speeding up software R&D.If we assume overall AI progress comes from ⅔ software and ⅓ hardware, then we get that speeding up the overall pace of progress by 1.7x requires speeding up software progress by 2.05x.49Then if we assume that software progress faces diminishing returns where each year of software progress is twice as hard, and that there has been an additional ~0.6 years of software progress, then you get that software R&D uplift is (2.05 * 2^0.6 =) 3.1x in Nov 2026.50If we assume that as of May 2026 uplift was ~1.45x based on converting a ~1.2x AI-attributed pace of progress acceleration,51 and that SAR will correspond to a 25x uplift according to the AI Futures Model,52 or ~45x according to the SAR central estimate from the section above,53 then we can do a naive exponential extrapolation:This estimate is conservative in that it doesn’t account for automation speeding up the trend. However, it is extremely uncertain, given that we only have 2 data points which are both based on the METR report’s rough guesses. And the May data point is a very rough educated guess, rather than something explicitly stated by METR.We measure progress in 2027 as the ECI gained during 2027, in units of the average yearly ECI gain over 2024–25. Today's overall pace is ~2x (~1.7x AI-attributed), so if it held flat, 2027 would contain ~2 years of progress.The AI Futures Model, filtered to runs with a ~1.2x AI-attributed pace on May 1 2026 and ~1.7x on Nov 1 2026, instead gives a median of ~5 years with Daniel's parameters and ~4 with Eli's:METR described its range informally ("we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate"), so we don't know what interval they meant.1By Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) we mean: “an AI that matches the research taste of the best human researchers at an AGI company and can fully automate its coding.”2We define it more precisely here.3We also think we are likely to see something like 5 years’ worth of historical AI progress in 2027 (50% CI: 2.7 to 25 years). This is based on filtering the AI Futures Model with Daniel’s parameters to condition on 1.7x pace of progress in Nov 2026 and 1.2x in May.5We also recommend this piece which also analyzes the implications of the METR report.6It wasn’t just our predictions about the future that were too low; we also now think our estimates of the pace of progress in August 2026 were too low. Also note that this was the prediction implied by the model and parameters assigned by specific people, which may well have been lower than their all-things-considered view if they had been specifically asked about this question.7While the simple research extrapolation has a median Sep 2026 research taste of 1.5 SDs below the median AGI company researcher.8The ECI trend in the trajectory doesn’t match the AECI historical trajectory well, because the AIFM can’t model a slope increase that was initially mostly from non-AI-attributable factors.9METR writes: “We guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI. This judgment is given with substantial uncertainty, but is based on a variety of lines of evidence on contributions from AI and other causes. We believe AI’s contribution has grown relatively more important over time, and do not think the other factors we investigated would explain the sustained acceleration. The evidence of speedup from the usage of AI we describe below also seems compatible with a large contribution.” 1.7 is roughly 80% of the way to 2 from the baseline rate of progress in log space. More on this in an appendix.10METR says: “We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute.” Based on what we can determine externally from financial reporting, it seems like R&D compute grew around 3x 2024 → 2025 and 4.2x 2025 → 2026 (accounting for changes in allocation).11The baseline is roughly 14 points per year, and 14*1.7=24/year is achieved roughly in April.12Note that the AI does not need to dominate humans across every subskill of research taste. It is enough for the AI to have research taste such that the AI company would overall prefer to use only AIs for research taste than to use only copies of top humans for research taste (more precisely, the copies would have aggregate research taste as good as the top human, while retaining the same distribution of specializations as current human researchers).13Or actually, R&D parity only requires research taste slightly below average because coding skills will be ahead.14However, the acceleration being AI-attributable is evidence for more aggressive research taste level and slope parameters.15Claude estimates based on the charts in the report that it was internally deployed on roughly Sep 25.16My best guess is that AIs aren’t yet contributing enough via taste that we have that much evidence about the taste slope via an update toward more gradual acceleration. However: (a) it’s plausible to me that AIs are starting to contribute to taste in some sense, via mechanisms like (1) better integrating information across teams leading to more fruitful experiment ideas or (2) brainstorming lots of ideas quickly and (b) even if the taste is currently quite low, I can hackily represent the general update toward slower takeoff based on gradual acceleration via lowering the taste slope here.17Time to SAR is the remaining taste gap divided by the slope, so draws where Model 4 is already near or past SAR arrive early almost regardless of the slope, while draws with a large gap are pulled earlier by a steep slope about as often as they're pushed later by a shallow one.18I think the top researcher is much more valuable than the median researcher. The difference between the 99.9th percentile and average of a lognormal distribution with median 1 and 99.9th percentile 1,000 is ~80x (the average is ~12x the median).19k is directly proportional to r, i.e. the number of doublings of software efficiency you get from a doubling of cumulative research. In the terms of Economics of RSI, k = ln 2 × r × ε_C,A. (With ε_C,A ≈ 3.9 AECI points per e-fold in our calibration; the paper's 6.5 is for Epoch's ECI).20Also called ε_R,C, and "research effort's elasticity to AI capabilities”.21I.e., I’ll assume that d is itself a linear function of ECI going forward.22These numbers imply that r (doublings of software efficiency per doublings of research) is roughly 3.3, and that k is roughly 9 AECI points per doubling of research.23From the labor uplift section above: raising all researchers to the research taste of the best researcher is worth ~100x (the top researcher vs. the average researcher), or ~500x after accounting for complementarity between AIs and humans; fully automating coding is worth ~2,000x; together that is ~1,000x AI R&D labor uplift at SAR. To convert labor uplift into software R&D uplift, we use Ryan Greenblatt’s production function for software progress, labor^0.55 * compute^0.45, with experiment compute held fixed: 1,000^0.55 = ~45x. With his alternative exponents of 0.3 and 0.7 instead of 0.55, this would be ~8x or ~125x.24The exponential fit behind line E seems implausible since I’d expect d to be increasing as AI becomes more important for software R&D.25While scaling the total amount of acceleration to hold the fraction of AI acceleration fixed at 80%.26See the very last section for a description of how the number is calculated from the other parameters he estimates.27We’re working with little evidence here, including: (a) the description of even the acceleration in late 2025 as “likely influenced by non-AI factors,” implying AI plausibly had a role, (b) the suggestive “fake data” graph, (c) interviewed researchers describe Mythos Preview (internal ~Apr 2026) as a big jump (“a sharp inflection”), and (d) staff self-reported uplift was ~4x for Mythos Preview and ~5x for Mythos 5 (Jun) vs ~12x for Model 4 (Oct).28We correspondingly shift the confidence interval. It’s now an 80% confidence interval of [0.40, 5.61], median 1.5.30The coding-only uplift should be higher than the overall labor uplift because coding is relatively easy to automate. This is pricing in some amount of self-report overestimation. The (uplift-1) doubling time in the trajectory is set to 3.3 months, very similar to the 3.4 months one gets from fitting to self-reports.31I’m imagining here a very simplified model of AI R&D which includes only 3 tasks with equal weight: experiment implementation, research taste, and data generation. If data generation “merely” was as automated as coding is, then it would provide some additional acceleration but it probably couldn’t bring up a 1.25x AI-attributed acceleration to 1.7x.32Referring specifically to the non-AI-attributable component of the acceleration.33This is done by changing taste at AC and taste slope; AC held at late Dec 2026.34They ended up thinking that “internal evidence provided support for there being significant acceleration in Anthropic’s model training pipeline”.35And then, if there’s any set of capabilities that loop back on the ability to further improve those capabilities, and this effect is large enough to cause accelerating, hyperbolic growth, then things could go very far. And given sufficiently large progress in any domain like that, it seems very likely that those capabilities can also be applied to cause more general progress shortly thereafter. (See e.g. the arguments about “Data bottlenecks to automating real-world work” here.)36We expect this METR team to publish their work in the next couple of days.37But it’s possible that further investigation could provide new evidence that would change our mind in more substantive ways. For example, evidence about whether acceleration is larger or smaller on different task distributions could be informative for whether recent progress is likely to generalize far enough to feed back into itself.39Both our specific parameterizations, but also to some extent the model structure.41Of the ~6-month shift (~7.5 months with the larger gap), centering at 1.6x rather than 1.7x accounts for about 2–2.5 months (2–3.5 with the larger gap) and the spread for the other 3.5–4 months (4–5.5), depending on which is applied first. Each piece carries roughly ±1.5–3 months of sampling noise, so the split is rough. The spread pushes later because TED-AI timing is asymmetric in acceleration: the chance of TED-AI by the end of 2027 is 53% for trajectories at about 1.6x, but 26% at 1.18–1.35x and 2% below 1.06x, versus 68% at 1.84–3x and 79% at 3–6.5x. The distribution puts 38% of its weight below 1.35x, so mixing lowers the chance of TED-AI by the end of 2027 from 53% to 47%.42This distribution puts 18% of its weight above 3x (vs. 25% for 1 + 0.6 [0.06, 6] clipped at 7) and 10% at the 5x clip. It gives a 59% chance of SAR by the end of 2027 (vs. 67%) and 40% for TED-AI (vs. 47%), or 36% (vs. 43%) with the larger gap. With the same distribution, Daniel’s parameters give SAR in May 2027 and TED-AI in Oct 2027 (vs. Mar 2027 and Jul 2027), and Brendan’s give Jun 2027 and Apr 2028 (vs. Mar 2027 and Nov 2027). TED-AI medians carry roughly ±1–2.5 months of sampling noise.45Current training runs probably require a small fraction of frontier companies’ total compute, meaning that even if the training recipe/IP (but not the model weights) are stolen, a Chinese company like ByteDance could use a larger fraction of its total compute (e.g. 50% instead of 10%), and train for twice as long (e.g. 6 months instead of 3 months), and end up with SAR just a few months after the US companies do.46This is done by changing taste at AC and taste slope; AC held at late Nov 2026.47Based on the AI Futures Model with Daniel's parameters. We filtered to trajectories where AI software R&D uplift is about 1.7x on Nov 1, 2026, meaning AI multiplies software research effort by 1.7x compared with no AI. In those trajectories the median pace of overall AI progress on that date is 1.11x (50% CI: 1.05–1.19x) the trajectory's own Jan 2024 – Jul 2025 pace.48Same method, filtered to trajectories where AI makes coding labor about 1.7x faster on Nov 1, 2026. The model has no separate multiplier for research labor as a whole, so we use serial coding labor uplift as the proxy. The median pace of overall progress is 1.03x (50% CI: 1.00–1.07x) the Jan 2024 – Jul 2025 pace.49(⅔)x + (⅓) = 1.7. So 2x + 1 = 5.1. x = (5.1-1)/2 = 2.05. With Ryan's ~2x, this gives 2.5x.50Ryan: “I've previously estimated software R&D would slow down by around 2x for each year of software progress if you held inputs fixed and based on the report, it seems as though we've perhaps seen roughly 0.35-1.0 years of additional software progress incorporated into trained models so far (geometric mean of ~0.6).” This also roughly matches what we get in the filtered AI Futures Model runs (3.3x for Daniel, 3.8x for Eli). With Ryan's ~2x pace instead of 1.7x, the calculation above gives 3.8x.51Using the same method as for Nov 2026: the 1.2x pace of progress on May 1 2026 that we use elsewhere in this post implies a (3 * 1.2 - 1) / 2 = 1.3x software pace. For diminishing returns, we assume software pace ramped up linearly from 1x on Jul 1 2025 to 1.3x on May 1 and 2.05x on Nov 1, and scale it so the total by Nov 1 matches Ryan’s ~0.6 years. About a quarter of that, ~0.16 years, had accumulated by May 1, so uplift was 1.3 * 2^0.16 = ~1.45x. Ignoring diminishing returns gives 1.3x.52In the unfiltered AI Futures Model, the median uplift is 3.3x at AC and 18x at SAR with Daniel's parameters (4.1x and 19x with Eli's). We seem to have hit ~3x without hitting AC, so we assume a 10% chance that AC has already happened. Taking runs filtered to match METR's ~1.7x acceleration and reweighting them so that 10% have reached AC by Nov 1 2026, the median uplift is 5.9x at AC and 24x at SAR with Daniel's parameters (6.9x and 21x with Eli's).53From the labor uplift section above: raising all researchers to the research taste of the best researcher is worth ~100x (the top researcher vs. the average researcher), or ~500x after accounting for complementarity between AIs and humans; fully automating coding is worth ~2,000x; together that is ~1,000x AI R&D labor uplift at SAR. To convert labor uplift into software R&D uplift, we use Ryan Greenblatt’s production function for software progress, labor^0.55 * compute^0.45, with experiment compute held fixed: 1,000^0.55 = ~45x. With his alternative exponents of 0.3 and 0.7 instead of 0.55, this would be ~8x or ~125x.

blocks.html_en: If SAR is coming in 2027, it is incredibly urgent to pause or substantially ‘pace’ frontier AI development, with the ideal being an industry-wide pause followed by an international agreement. Companies are not on track to align a SAR, and using a misaligned SAR to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) will put us in an extremely bad position. Additionally, if we train SAR in the near future, China will probably be able to steal the training recipe and maybe even the model weights (more).5

blocks.html_en:
• Pace of progress acceleration is how much faster AI progress is advancing in present day, compared to a baseline reference period (in Anthropic’s case, the baseline is “the fastest rate of extended progress we’ve observed in the absence of significant AI contributions to AI R&D”). It is usually much lower than AI software R&D uplift because (a) it is subject to diminishing returns to more software R&D and (b) it includes compute scaling.

    • The compute scaling point is simple: Part of the reason why modern AIs are smarter than older AIs is literally that they are bigger, trained longer, etc. More compute goes in, more capability comes out. As AI companies build more datacenters they unlock the ability to make larger AIs and train them longer. Since overall progress comes partly from software R&D and partly from compute scaling, a doubling in software R&D will cause less than a doubling in overall progress.

    • To expand on the diminishing returns point: AI software progress in general is subject to diminishing returns; the low-hanging fruit gets picked first, and to keep finding better and better algorithms requires exponentially more investment (more and bigger experiments, more and smarter researchers thinking for longer, etc.). Historically, the AI industry has scaled up R&D investments in a way that’s roughly cancelled out these diminishing returns. But the point here is, to get two years of research progress in one year, you have to more than double the AI software R&D uplift.

blocks.html_en: A SAR is an AI that, if dropped into an AGI project in present day, would be as good at research taste as the project would be if there were only human researchers, who were each made as competent at research taste as the top researcher.12 The SAR must also qualify as an Automated Coder (AC), i.e., be able to fully automate coding in the AGI project. [By research taste, we mean the ability to select research directions and experiments, and interpret their results.]

sentences.en: A SAR is an AI that, if dropped into an AGI project in present day, would be as good at research taste as the project would be if there were only human researchers, who were each made as competent at research taste as the top researcher.12 The SAR must also qualify as an Automated Coder (AC), i.e., be able to fully automate coding in the AGI project. [By research taste, we mean the ability to select research directions and experiments, and interpret their results.]

blocks.html_en: It’s a somewhat stronger condition than AI R&D parity, the point at which the company would rather fire their human researchers than fire their AIs, because the research taste must be at the level of the top human rather than the average.13 If one wishes not to rely on our abstraction of research taste, then you can think of our SAR arrival dates as upper bounds for when AI R&D parity will be reached.

blocks.html_en: • The toy model effectively assumes that the exogenous inputs were constant, and assumes that the growth of [AI software R&D uplift] was large enough to both overcome diminishing returns and to increase the rate of ECI/y by 1.7x. However, in reality, the research produced during 2026 was due to a combination of an increase in the growth rate of [AI software R&D uplift] and the normal growth of exogenous inputs. The fact that exogenous inputs still grew at their normal rate cancelled out a lot of the diminishing returns, which means that the growth rate of AI software R&D uplift needed to increase somewhat less in order to achieve the 1.7x increase in ECI/y. (Relative to how much it would have had to increase without the ‘normal’ growth in exogenous inputs.) Taking this into account, we will infer lower values of dk, and dk>1 is less likely.

However, in reality, the research produced during 2026 was due to a combination of an increase in the growth rate of [AI software R&D uplift] and the normal growth of exogenous inputs. The fact that exogenous inputs still grew at their normal rate cancelled out a lot of the diminishing returns, which means that the growth rate of AI software R&D uplift needed to increase somewhat less in order to achieve the 1.7x increase in ECI/y. (Relative to how much it would have had to increase without the ‘normal’ growth in exogenous inputs.) Taking this into account, we will infer lower values of dk, and dk>1 is less likely.

blocks.html_en: Moreover, there are various other sources of evidence that have accumulated since our previous timelines update that seem to corroborate the overall sense that timelines are shorter than we thought. For example, the Mathopocalypse seems to be evidence of many extremely long-horizon math problems being solved autonomously by AI. Another example: People we know who work at AI companies are saying that timelines are indeed very short and that RSI is imminent, even more than they were before, and much more than historically (remember, when AI 2027 came out most of our friends in industry said it depicted AI capabilities growing too fast). blocks.html_en:
• If the models do still have significant weaknesses, and those weaknesses are a significant bottleneck for them, then seeing substantial acceleration despite that means that AI R&D must be really easy to increase by increasing (automated) labor. (For example, it means that compute is less of a bottleneck than expected.) In other words, it would mean there’s a lot of low-hanging fruit to pick by automated labor even when that labor has weaknesses that are causing serious problems.

    • This predicts even faster progress, because the implication is that marginal increases in automation will probably yield progressively larger speedups, as each bottleneck gets removed and each remaining bottleneck gets more important.

    • For illustration: In the extreme of maximal bottlenecking dynamics, where automated tasks can be done infinitely fast and unautomated tasks are the only things holding progress back, speedup goes to infinity like 1/(1-x) as automation fraction x goes to 1.

Maybe you had a prior that some specific set of tasks (e.g. coding) were going to be easy, leading to a moderate speed-up of the overall pace of progress, but the further capabilities needed for additional speed-up are much more difficult. blocks.html_en: The AIFM doesn’t take into account the discrete nature of training runs, which could overestimate takeoff speeds. In other words, the AIFM assumes that a new innovation will be instantly applied to models and then cause further speed-ups in the rate of innovation discovery. But in practice, it might take months for pretraining improvements to show up in a fully trained model, and perhaps weeks for RL training improvements to show up. Our rough, intuition-based best guess is that this pushes back the SAR median by about 1–3 months relative to the AIFM’s predictions. However, this concern does not apply to the model based on linear extrapolation, since it does not rely on further speed-ups from here.

blocks.html_en: In the Q2.5 timelines update written mid-August, I said my 50% mark for AC was December 2027 and my 50% mark for SAR was December 2028. Since then various pieces of evidence have appeared and weighed on my mind, including industry insider rumors, public statements by AI companies, the mathopocalypse, and even the Hugging Face incident which was an example of AIs doing research projects end-to-end. The biggest single piece of evidence, however, is this METR report. I still don’t trust it completely, of course, and so I still have substantial credence that things will turn out to take longer than the models and trendlines naively imply for one reason or another. But on the other hand, it’s also scarily plausible that things will go even faster than the models or trendlines naively imply, for several reasons. For example, humans in general might have a bias towards underestimating AI capabilities progress – this certainly seems true outside the AI industry, but even within the AI industry it seems more have underestimated it than overestimated it historically. Unless this bias somehow doesn’t apply to Anthropic or METR today, then, it seems we should try to correct for it, but that would mean SAR is happening this winter!?!? At any rate, mashing together all these factors, it seems to me that I should roughly go with what the naive extrapolations and models say – so, let’s say May 2027 for SAR median, i.e., 50% chance of SAR by May 2027.

sentences.en: In the Q2.5 timelines update written mid-August, I said my 50% mark for AC was December 2027 and my 50% mark for SAR was December 2028.

Since then various pieces of evidence have appeared and weighed on my mind, including industry insider rumors, public statements by AI companies, the mathopocalypse, and even the Hugging Face incident which was an example of AIs doing research projects end-to-end.
The biggest single piece of evidence, however, is this METR report.
I still don’t trust it completely, of course, and so I still have substantial credence that things will turn out to take longer than the models and trendlines naively imply for one reason or another.
But on the other hand, it’s also scarily plausible that things will go even faster than the models or trendlines naively imply, for several reasons.

For example, humans in general might have a bias towards underestimating AI capabilities progress – this certainly seems true outside the AI industry, but even within the AI industry it seems more have underestimated it than overestimated it historically.
Unless this bias somehow doesn’t apply to Anthropic or METR today, then, it seems we should try to correct for it, but that would mean SAR is happening this winter!?!?

At any rate, mashing together all these factors, it seems to me that I should roughly go with what the naive extrapolations and models say – so, let’s say May 2027 for SAR median, i.e., 50% chance of SAR by May 2027.

• I think the METR report in aggregate, if correct, is significant evidence for SAR before EOY 2027.

    • However, the METR report on its own does not have sufficient data in it to support that claim (because of redactions).

    • One load-bearing subclaim of the METR report, for which the supporting evidence isn’t public, is that the observed AECI trend shift is: (i) currently 80% downstream of AI uplift, and (ii) not largely downstream of AI uplift earlier in the year (despite the graph appearing to have a one-time change in slope).

    • The AECI data is an aggregate of benchmark scores. I think there are other explanations for a rapid increase in benchmark scores besides large AI acceleration. For example, I think this is a plausible explanation of the AECI acceleration. (The AECI acceleration is downstream of shifting compute to RL, which more directly increases benchmark scores than pretraining improvements.)

    • I would be much more confident if more of the relevant data was public. For example, it would be extremely useful to understand how much algorithmic progress has been made at AI companies, as well as the form of the algorithmic progress. If there was a significant increase in the rate of algorithmic progress that was clearly attributable to AI, and we saw a similar change in slope to the AECI numbers, that would be strong supporting evidence.

    • My all-things-considered view is that METR is probably right, and if we were to see all of the evidence, we would probably see significant acceleration of other metrics such as algorithmic progress, and that this would support the claims made in the METR report. Public statements from labs echo this. E.g. Dario says: “My first concern is that, since roughly this summer, AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI’s growing ability to build the next generation of AI.”

• The other big things on my mind are math and cyber AIs.

    • It seems like around Mythos, AIs became superhuman at vulnerability discovery, and around Astra, AIs became superhuman at mathematics. Both of those domains are cheaply verifiable.

    • I think the difference between Math/Cyber and AI is a (relatively small) quantitative difference, not a difference in kind. The swarm that solved Navier-Stokes was operating fully autonomously, and was able to benefit from ~10k agents running in parallel. The main difference is that with AI research, you need to do experiments in order to verify correctness. Pretraining validation loss seems to be a relatively straightforward and extremely strong predictor of general purpose capabilities. I don’t see strong barriers to full automation of pretraining research, and post-training research seems only mildly harder.

    • I think the recent history of verifiable fields falling indicates a reasonably high likelihood of AI R&D falling in the near future as well.

• However, I do think that the METR report should mostly update us about “how hard is it to make AIs help with AI research” and somewhat less about how far away key milestones like SAR, TED-AI and superintelligence are.

    • This is because I generally have also updated towards more spikiness in AI capabilities. It seems like there are some domains where AI progress has moved extremely quickly, and others where it has moved slowly, more so than I would’ve expected. I think this is largely explained by there being a broad range of difficulty levels to training AI to be good in different domains.

    • I think we have seen this in Navier–Stokes, Hugging Face, coding, etc. while frontier models still feel like they are dumb in a lot of ways. Also internal Model 4 does not seem like it's made a huge jump on AECI above Opus 5.5, so I don’t expect this to be different internally.

• My ATC view on how much progress we will see in 2027 is largely informed by the AIFM, but not the time to SAR and TED-AI which depend on shaky estimates about the current research taste of models and how much they will improve.

• To better inform my ATC view on how far away SAR and TED-AI are, I've made a variation of the AIFM that accounts for ‘taste spikiness’.

    • This variation treats research taste and economically relevant tasks as a 0-100 task continuum, parametrized by the hardest-to-easiest gap, instead of single numbers.

    • AI research taste bottlenecks very lightly, because I think a lot of progress can be made without being super good at all areas of AI research (the tasks combine almost as a geometric mean, ρ = −0.2).

    • The hardest-to-easiest gap between domains is set to be a median of 5x for AI research and 10x for all economically relevant tasks

    • In both continuums, my guess is that the typical task is at −2 SD today (AIFM's 1.7x-filtered runs have +0.7 SD on Nov 1; the post's best guess is −1.5 SD on Sep 25, 2026), with levels spread ±2.5 SD. The typical task improves at AIFM's own taste slope (median 2.4 SD per 2025-year in Eli's parameters), and other tasks' rates are spread around it by the hardest-to-easiest gap. Runs are resampled to my METR distribution (median 1.7x, 90% CI 1.3–3.0x) using my variation's own Nov 1 pace, not AIFM's.

    • SAR is reached when an AI-only company would be as good at research taste as a company of humans who keep their relative strengths but are each as good overall as the top researcher: the research tasks, combined with a somewhat stronger bottleneck than in the dynamics (ρ = −0.5), reach the top researcher's overall level, and AIFM's automated coder is reached. TED-AI is reached when 95% of economically relevant tasks are at the top-expert level (99.9th percentile).

• I have various other feelings that I could list (including some overlap with e.g., Eli’s points above) for reasons I think I should adjust upwards or downwards, including some listed below. I don’t think these strongly push me in any direction overall, so I am running with my variation of the AIFM above as representing my ATC view.

    • Hardware progress might make the later years move faster than what the AIFM predicts.

    • There might be “1-3 more big pre-trains needed.” I have the vague sense that pre-training will be more important for generalization than post-training, and it might be really hard to improve AIs in some areas via post-training, so there might be a bit of a wave of progress after each big model scale up, and it might be increasingly hard to make up for lack of absolute compute scale up with algorithmic efficiency due to ideas getting harder, and it just generally being more favorable to have a bigger model to start from for post-training scaling laws.

blocks.html_en: Let’s say Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) is coming in 2027. What does that entail?

sentences.en: Let’s say Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) is coming in 2027.
What does that entail?

blocks.html_en: A SAR will be able to fully automate AI R&D, including matching the research taste of top humans. At this point, AI research might look kind of like math research does right now: most of the progress coming from fully autonomous agent swarms, with humans doing their best to decipher the AIs’ work. A SAR is past parity with humans, and likely close to the point where humans are adding very little value on top of the AIs.

sentences.en: A SAR will be able to fully automate AI R&D, including matching the research taste of top humans.

At this point, AI research might look kind of like math research does right now: most of the progress coming from fully autonomous agent swarms, with humans doing their best to decipher the AIs’ work.
A SAR is past parity with humans, and likely close to the point where humans are adding very little value on top of the AIs.

blocks.html_en: If a misaligned SAR is used to do RSI, we’re in a very bad position. Using a SAR to automate AI R&D with little human oversight, relying upon other models to monitor the SAR, is very scary. Our best guess is that if this is attempted, and the SAR is misaligned, the model that the SAR produces will be even more capable and still misaligned, putting us in an even worse position. SAR itself probably won’t be able to take over on its own, because we expect its capabilities to be jagged: superhuman at AI research but still weaker than humans at many other things. blocks.html_en: Avoiding “full RSI” by supposedly keeping a human in the loop, while rapidly improving capabilities anyway, would still be extremely dangerous. Anthropic said in their S-1: “We are also considering additional measures, including updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy, to require human review and approval of certain decisions in our research and development processes as our models perform an increasing share of that work.” While we support efforts to marginally increase human oversight, we worry that this sort of effort will provide too much comfort. Models are already producing way more outputs than humans are able to effectively review,44 and this will become much more true during RSI. Without very strong pacing, there simply won’t be enough time for humans to stay meaningfully in the loop, and we expect there to be strong pressures toward approving model actions that haven’t been fully understood.

blocks.html_en: Claude Opus 5.5 gives the following possible interpretations of METR’s claim that “we guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI.”

sentences.en: Claude Opus 5.5 gives the following possible interpretations of METR’s claim that “we guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI.”

blocks.html_en:
Let h, c, n be the historical, current (Oct 2026), and no-AI counterfactual growth rates, measured in whatever units progress is roughly linear in. For AECI that's points per year: the fitted trend went from about +15 points/year before October 2025 to about +29 after. For an exponential metric (as in METR's worked example) it's the log growth rate. METR's definitions give total acceleration A = c/h ≈ 2, acceleration due to AI a = c/n, and implicitly non-AI acceleration b = n/h, with A = a·b. The "≈80%" is a claim about where n sits between h and c. The readings differ in which yardstick measures that.

Reading 1: share of the slope change (additive). (c − n)/(c − h) = 0.8, so n = h + 0.2(c − h). In METR's "years of progress" units this is concrete. At A = 2, Anthropic makes about one extra historical-year of progress per calendar year, and about 0.8 of that extra year is due to AI. Without AI it would make about 1.2 historical-years per year, which implies a ≈ 1.67. This is probably what's intended. METR's illustrative chart labels the two gaps "excess growth due to AI" and "excess growth due to non-AI factors," it annotates the slope ΔAECI/Δtime, the AECI trends are fit linearly, and one interviewee framed it the same way, attributing 50–80% of the slope change to Claude.

Reading 2: share of the log-acceleration (multiplicative). ln a / ln A = 0.8, so a = A^0.8 ≈ 1.74 and b = A^0.2 ≈ 1.15. This is natural if you take METR's ratio definitions literally. Since a·b = A, the logs add exactly, so this split doesn't depend on which factor you remove first.

Reading 3: share of the excess multiplier. (a − 1)/(A − 1) = 0.8, so a = 1.8. It sounds natural ("AI provides 80% of the extra speedup"), but it isn't a decomposition. The non-AI share computed the same way is (b − 1)/(A − 1) ≈ 11%, so the two shares sum to 91%. An even more naive reading, a/A = 0.8, fails outright: if AI did nothing, a = 1 and you'd still get 1/A = 50%.

blocks.html_en:
The readings agree near A ≈ 1, because ln x ≈ x − 1 there, and they diverge as A grows. At METR's central estimate the spread is modest. In METR's own illustrative numbers (h = ln 2, n = ln 3, c = ln 9), AI's share comes out to 73%, 60%, or 46% under readings 1, 2, and 3. The same picture could be described as "a majority" or "a minority" depending on the yardstick.

Why 1 versus 2 is really a modeling choice. If AI and other factors add to the growth rate (c = h + Δ_AI + Δ_other), reading 1 is the clean split. If they multiply (c = h·a·b, for example because AI multiplies the productivity of whatever headcount, compute, and data you have), reading 1 becomes order-dependent. The counterfactual "remove AI, keep the non-AI factors" gives AI the entire interaction term h(a − 1)(b − 1). A Shapley split of the same numbers (A = 2, b = 1.2) gives AI about 73%, not 80%. Reading 2 has no such ambiguity under a multiplicative model.

blocks.html_en: AI software R&D progress is the rate at which the AI company is improving the algorithms it uses to train models. However, training better models requires both algorithms and training compute. If we were making AI software R&D progress 1.7x faster than normal, this would accelerate the algorithms but not the compute that goes into the final training runs, so the overall pace of progress would be less than 1.7x. We estimate that accelerating AI software R&D by 1.7x would only accelerate overall progress by about 1.1x.47

blocks.html_en:
Takeaway: a fix to how the AI Futures Model converts the research taste slope moves the filtered results slightly earlier and barely changes anything else.

What changed: the taste slope is input as SDs/2025-year, but the model converted it using each trajectory’s pace of progress at present day (end of July 2026) rather than mid-2025. In trajectories that had already accelerated, like the filtered ones (1.2–1.4x the 2024–mid-2025 rate), this made the effective slope 20–30% lower than the parameter value. In typical trajectories the two rates match (median ratio 1.01). The conversion now uses the pace at mid-2025 (new parameter taste_slope_reference_date, default 2025.5).

Effect: Daniel’s preset barely moves (SAR one week earlier). p(SAR by EO2027) goes from 72% to 77% (1.5x), 87% to 90% (1.7x), 88% to 92% (1.7x Nov 1, 1.2x May 1) and 95% to 96% (2x). The joint median SAR moves from Apr to Mar 2027; the other SAR medians are unchanged to the month, and TED-AI medians move up to a month earlier. The partial coding automation trajectory’s SAR moves from Jun to May 2027. The one-time-beta-decrease trajectory barely moves (still Mar 2027), because the conversion reads a mapping that excludes the beta shift (rate ratio 1.04).

This appendix shows the fit behind the “TasteVal slope, AECI basis” row of the one-at-a-time table. TasteVal (arXiv 2610.06824) measures each model’s compute multiplier: the experiment compute the expert baseline needs to match the model’s final score, as a multiple of the model’s own compute budget. METR’s chart gives AECI only for Anthropic models, so each TasteVal model gets the AECI that METR’s fitted trend gives at its release date (+15 points per year before the October 7, 2025 break, +29 after; second plot). Release dates are read off TasteVal’s Figure 1.

We fit log(compute multiplier) against this AECI for the 17 frontier models TasteVal fits (GPT-4 to Opus 5.5), allowing one change in slope at the model where it best fits the data (largest Chow F-statistic, as TasteVal does). The change falls at GPT-5.2 (AECI ≈ 155, December 2025), the same model as in TasteVal’s own fits against release date and ECI. Before it, the multiplier doubled every 19.5 AECI points; since then, every 7.2 points (90% CI 5.4–9.0 from resampling the 11 post-break models). As a check, the same fit against release date reproduces TasteVal’s 3.0-month doubling time, which is about 7.2 points at 29 AECI points per year. A continuous kinked line gives 6.7 points per doubling. Using METR’s measured AECI for the six Anthropic models instead of the trend values gives 7.9, and fitting those six models alone, without a break, gives 5.6.
